Episcoporum acceptarent; at non hanc, fed aliam, cum variis nempe restrictionibus, distinctionibus sensuum, exposcebat Cavalerius. Ad extremum deposita omni verecundia per Tremoillium varia postulata Papæ ab opponentibus exposita, & inter hæc Concilium nationale, a quo, ut appellatio ad Generale fieri posset, pro fundamento stabilire ausi sunt. Verum Clemens, his tricis, & fraudibus ut finem imponeret, paucis respondit: duas superesse vias finiendæ compositionis, spontaneam submissionem, vel vim Canonicam. Sicque terminata fuit Cavalerii negotiatio.

§. 4.
*Appellatio ad Concilium Generale.*

Vaticana jam parabantur fulmina: Noaillius ab ipso Cardinalium Collegio purpura indignus censebatur. Nihilominus datum tempus adhuc resipiscendi, ex spe, quam ostenderant Opponentes confecto quodam doctrinæ schemate, quod cum ab acceptantibus probatum non fuit, scriptum eis trium columnarum, Janseniano illi olim simile obtulerunt, in quarum media ipsæ propositiones Quesnelli, ex una parte sensus obvius, ex altera alius quispiam Catholicus, vel certe excusationis patiens

Sed nec istud placere potuit, additæque ab acceptantibus glossæ, quibus ostendebant, & sensum obvium propositionum recte damnatum, & alterum eas, nisi per violentam detorsionem habere non posse. Ne tamen una cum hoc negotio spes omnis iterum intercideret, Cardinalis Rohanus Aurelianensem permovit, ut ad 20. Nov. 1716. conventum Episcoporum indiceret, in quo Acceptantes aliquam explicationem Bullæ proponerent. Id ægerrime tulit Pontifex, & omni modo hoc consilium impedire aggressus, duo Brevia misit, unum Duci, quid Noaillio pararet, significans, alterum Sorbonæ, cui facultates & omnia privilegia ad tempus suspendit: cumque Tremoillius Cardinalibus, qui alias literas cum amicissimis hortatibus ad Noaillium dederant, & Papæ ipsi persuadere vellet, ut quidpiam de danda vel admittenda quadam explicatione adderetur; hic tertium Breve adjecit ad Episcopos acceptantes, quo eos hortatus est, ne se ab Opponentibus decipi sinant, & neque ullam a se Bullæ explicationem expectarent, nec ipsimet darent, aut admitterent. Verum Aurelianensis Cardinalium literas Noaillio non exhibuit, qui interea Parlamento Duacensi, quod Theses quasdam Constitutioni faventes suppressisset…

§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The bolts of the Vatican were already being prepared: Noailles was judged unworthy of the purple by the College of Cardinals itself. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having finished a certain draft of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by the acceptors, they offered them a document of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which the propositions of Quesnell were read, on one side the obvious meaning, on the other some other Catholic [meaning], or at least one patient of excuse

 That you enjoy an excellent republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been spent, there can be nothing that I might long enjoy. But your era, which is on a better course, looks to the future for many things which it may rightly promise itself by entrusting the magistracies. If, however, there is anything in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only take up all labors bravely for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal mind, and I will consider myself to have received enough fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I hold to be most excellent and most ample, to your descendants along with you. If, however, it does not turn out by my service, I will rejoice that the greatest and most wise men are found in your city, who, by the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, however, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You, who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, will consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you decide regarding it, I will consider it good. Farewell.

I have decided to write to you what I think regarding the public utility of our citizens and in what way that matter can best be conducted by us, so that I might open the reasoning of all my counsels to you first. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city can be increased to the greatest extent without any inconvenience to our citizens or allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your opinion and prudence. You do not ignore that for many years before, neither merchants nor publicans (I call them pirates) could safely sail this sea of ours, from which it happened that our revenues sold for much less. It happens that they do not commit themselves to the danger willingly, since the greater part of the comforts arrives to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expenditure. Just as our sense was accustomed to happen in light matters, so after those things were disturbed and cast down, by which you and your fellow citizens had flourished for a long time, I am moved with no less disturbed spirit, as if it had happened to my own affairs, for what can be called more mine than what is yours? ### Concerning the seven theological and cardinal virtues

Ninth, I sinned by omission, because I neglected to keep the three theological and four cardinal virtues. In me, there is not true faith in Christ with good works. In me, there is not certain hope regarding future celestial goods. ¶ In me, there is not charity, which loves God above all things, and I have not loved my neighbor as myself. In me, there is not prudence, because I did not perform my actions when and how I ought to have done them, and I acted in my deeds incautiously according to the desires of pleasure. In me, there is not fortitude, because I did not manfully subjugate interior and exterior passions for Christ. I did not fear to do shameful and embarrassing things. ¶ In me, there is not temperance, because I did not wish to endure labors, fasts, and tribulations. ¶ In me, there is not justice, because I did not turn away from evil, but I neglected to do the good I was bound to do. I did not justly give to each one what was his.

Non hic viri hujus vitæ historiam texere lubet, duo tantum iis, quæ jam de eo dicta sunt, memoratu digna juvat addere. Primum est scriptum quoddam ab ipso Quesnello Sacerdoti cuidam missum, qui abstersa tandem errorum caligine, sibi, & Ecclesiæ redditus illud prodidit. Regulæ erant 12. articulis comprehensæ, quibus sui in conversatione inter se & cum vario hominum genere uterentur. Summa ferme hæc erat: Unio, & concordia: arcani fides: circumspectio in sermone pro varia hominum conditione: amphibologia in variis capitibus Religionis: uti Christum in Eucharistia præsentem, neque tantum per fidem, aut figuram, ut heterodoxi, sed neque per transubstantiationem, aut substantialiter, sive realiter, ut Catholici ajunt, dici volebat: quomodo igitur? modo imperceptibili. In Sacramento pænitentiæ attritionis insufficientiam, & necessitatem contritionis perfectæ urgerent. Gratiam sufficientem, libertatem indifferentiæ, merita modo aperte impugnarent, modo per verborum ambages, ut pressis exitus pateat: Gratiam victricem unice extollant: & sic alia plura. Alterum est

left:
…add two things to what has already been said about him that are worth noting. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain priest, who, having finally wiped away the mist of errors and being returned to himself and to the Church, produced it. They were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum of it was almost this: Union and concord; fidelity to the secret; circumspection in speech according to the various conditions of men; ambiguity in various chapters of Religion; he wanted it to be said that Christ is present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox say, but neither by transubstantiation, nor substantially or really, as the Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible way. In the Sacrament of Penance, they would urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They would openly attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, sometimes directly and sometimes through the maze of words, so that an exit might be open for the pressured: let them exalt only victorious grace: and so many other things.

———— page break ————

The second is a notable testimony of truth given by the man himself. Quesnel, asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party of those then litigating about matters of Religion he should adhere, responded by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he himself had not been provoked and compelled to foster these disputes so pertinaciously except by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had heard the same from Quesnel's own mouth not only once, with the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, as witness in his *Reflexions consolatoires* . But from the time when madness swept the man away, in the year 1719, at the very end of his old age in Amsterdam and brought to the borders of death, four days before his passing, he renewed his appeal, having summoned two witnesses, and thus, having received viaticum from his Pastor, the old man lived on until December 2.

It is easy to divine with what sense of grief the faction saw its nest disturbed so suddenly. First there was huge trepidation, then cries: on one side torments and mournful laments of those who deplored the persecution of truth and innocence; on the other side, curses of those who denounced all that was of sacred and profane dignity; finally, there was tumult among the very parts of the faction, and it was contested for many years of the present century. The other point is that he draws a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual law from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the Law, circumcised their own or others' children. Furthermore, this was also to the disgrace and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that action, argued that Moses was guilty of excessive negligence through his wife, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that most holy covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? For we never read that the task of circumcising was once specially mandated to the priests by God, since circumcision was instituted by God and practiced by the people for more than four hundred years, even before the priests were separated from the rest of the people. ### Concerning the seven theological and cardinal virtues

Ninth, I sinned by omission, because I neglected to keep the three theological and four cardinal virtues. In me, there is not true faith in Christ with good works. In me, there is not certain hope regarding future celestial goods. ¶ In me, there is not charity, which loves God above all things, and I have not loved my neighbor as myself. In me, there is not prudence, because I did not perform my actions when and how I ought to have done them, and I acted in my deeds incautiously according to the desires of pleasure. In me, there is not fortitude, because I did not manfully subjugate interior and exterior passions for Christ. I did not fear to do shameful and embarrassing things. ¶ In me, there is not temperance, because I did not wish to endure labors, fasts, and tribulations. ¶ In me, there is not justice, because I did not turn away from evil, but I neglected to do the good I was bound to do. I did not justly give to each one what was his.

…everyone served the times. If anyone divided the opinions, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. Now, however, we give ourselves to such studies for a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy, as they say, but the same that we received from our fathers, so that we might never live if not for ourselves, except in this time in which we now are. For a few who were oppressing the public liberty have been removed from the city, and all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to say what he feels about our republic, and to feel freely what he says. The studies that were applied to private matters have all been turned to the amplitude of the republic. And they are especially intent on this one thing, which is most profitable to the city. If, therefore, you desire to be considered great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we have as the best and most beautiful. You will be able to do as much in it as you will provide in labor, industry, and solicitude for the others. Farewell.

 That you use the best republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been passed, there can be nothing that I might use for long.

But your age, which is in a better course, looks to the future, for which it can rightly promise itself by being given magistrates. But if it does not turn out according to my duty, I will rejoice that the highest and most wise men are found in your city who, with the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, for my part, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you decide about it, I will consider it good. Farewell.

And I will judge myself to have received sufficient fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I consider the best and most ample, to your descendants along with you. If, however, it does not turn out according to my duty, I will rejoice that the greatest and wisest men are found in your city, who can protect the fatherland with the best laws and wisest institutions. I, for my part, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, will consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you determine concerning it, I will consider it good. Farewell.

For he conducts this cause so astutely that, while attributing great praises—both of singular piety toward God and of patience—to you (that is, the flock and little sheep, as he calls them), he ascribes the whole blame for the errors (in which, if it pleases God, he wishes the Gallic and reformed Churches of Christ to be entangled) to us, the Pastors. Thus he tries to tear us Pastors away from you, the sheep, and you, the sheep, away from us, the Pastors—that is, the most closely joined members of the same body—so that, just as he scattered those fatal discords in the midst of Germany, he might also be able to disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches on account of Ubiquity.*

# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

Osiander, so that you may know the man, is the diapyros and carrier of a certain new Pandora, manufactured by—I know not whom—Vulcan, which he has undertaken to carry off to other shores and provinces of the world, such as Gaul and Belgium. But he either thinks you are logs and stumps, to tolerate such bitter [charges] for so long, concerning a doctrine unknown to you and never weighed against the standard of the Divine word as a just scale; or, if he thinks you are pious and prudent, he ought surely to have thought well of you, and to have assumed that you had done what is written of the Beroeans and Thessalonians, namely, that you would search the scriptures and diligently compare our doctrine with them. Noailles was further terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In 1727, several bishops had gathered at Embrun to defeat the monstrous errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances they had incited. Furthermore, there were two primary acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer, from the monastery of Saint Genevieve, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who set out for England to carry out the system of Dupin and distinguished himself there with other writings regarding the ordinations of Anglican bishops; and second, the sentence passed on September 20th against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as Quesnel’s work was commended, the Bull condemning it was prostituted as worthy of all execration. ### Monday
### Nocturn

My Lady, may the splendor of your face be my illumination, and may the serenity of your grace shine upon my mind. Exalt my head above my enemies, and I shall sing; I shall chant a psalm to your name. Do not turn your face from me, for I have desired your hope and your beauty from my youth. I have loved you and sought your mercy, O Queen of Heaven; do not withdraw your grace from your servant. I will confess you among the nations, and I will honor the throne of your glory. Glory.

To you, Lady, I will call out and you will hear me; in the voice of your praise, you will gladden me. Have mercy on me in the day of my anguish, and in the light of your truth, deliver me. May you be blessed, O Lady, in all the ends of the globe of the earth. The sanctuary that your hands have established is the holy temple of your body. Your clean and immaculate conscience is the place

———— page break ————

of propitiation and the holy dwelling place of God. Bring to our Lady, O children of God, bring to our Lady praise and reverence. Grant strength to your servants, holy Mother, and blessing to those praising and glorifying you. Hear the groaning of those sighing to you, and do not spurn the vows of those invoking your name. May your hand be prepared to succor me, and may your ear be attentive to my supplication. May the heavens and the earth, the sea and the orb of the lands, bless you.

I will exalt you, Lady, for you have taken me up; you will deliver me from the iniquitous adversary. Turn to me and bring me to life; lead me back from the gates of death and from the floods of tribulations that have surrounded me. For the sake of yourself and the magnificence of your right hand, crush and dissipate all my adversaries. And I will offer you a sacrifice of praise, and I will exalt your glory more devotedly. Rejoice, heavens, and be glad, earth, for the Lady will console her own, and she will have mercy on her poor.

In you, Lady, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever. In your grace, take me up.

All good men were stunned until Saint-Andrè, Bossuet’s Vicar, who knew as a witness and arbiter everything that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most shameful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted; the work was denounced to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, by spreading seditious pamphlets through Belgium and France, as was related above—especially taking the opportunity from the aforementioned *Case of Conscience*—confounded everything. And now the unbridled license of those men seemed to need curbing by nothing less than the application of force. But this was the labor. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hiding places, clothes, and assumed names—now called Father Prior, or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had hitherto eluded the industry of the most sagacious men.

Non hic viri hujus vitæ historiam texere lubet, duo tantum iis, quæ jam de eo dicta sunt, memoratu digna juvat addere. Primum est scriptum quoddam ab ipso Quesnello Sacerdoti cuidam missum, qui abstersa tandem errorum caligine, sibi, & Ecclesiæ redditus illud prodidit. Regulæ erant 12. articulis comprehensæ, quibus sui in conversatione inter se & cum vario hominum genere uterentur. Summa ferme hæc erat: Unio, & concordia: arcani fides: circumspectio in sermone pro varia hominum conditione: amphibologia in variis capitibus Religionis: uti Christum in Eucharistia præsentem, neque tantum per fidem, aut figuram, ut heterodoxi, sed neque per transubstantiationem, aut substantialiter, sive realiter, ut Catholici ajunt, dici volebat: quomodo igitur? modo imperceptibili. In Sacramento pænitentiæ attritionis insufficientiam, & necessitatem contritionis perfectæ urgerent. Gratiam sufficientem, libertatem indifferentiæ, merita modo aperte impugnarent, modo per verborum ambages, ut pressis exitus pateat: Gratiam victricem unice extollant: & sic alia plura. Alterum est

…add two things to what has already been said about him that are worth noting. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain priest, who, having finally wiped away the mist of errors and being returned to himself and to the Church, produced it. They were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum of it was almost this: Union and concord; fidelity to the secret; circumspection in speech according to the various conditions of men; ambiguity in various chapters of Religion; he wanted it to be said that Christ is present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox say, but neither by transubstantiation, nor substantially or really, as the Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible way. In the Sacrament of Penance, they would urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They would openly attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, sometimes directly and sometimes through the maze of words, so that an exit might be open for the pressured: let them exalt only victorious grace: and so many other things.

———— page break ————

The second is a notable testimony of truth given by the man himself. Quesnel, asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party of those then litigating about matters of Religion he should adhere, responded by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he himself had not been provoked and compelled to foster these disputes so pertinaciously except by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had heard the same from Quesnel's own mouth not only once, with the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, as witness in his *Reflexions consolatoires* . But from the time when madness swept the man away, in the year 1719, at the very end of his old age in Amsterdam and brought to the borders of death, four days before his passing, he renewed his appeal, having summoned two witnesses, and thus, having received viaticum from his Pastor, the old man lived on until December 2.

### *Liber Jansenii editur, damnatur, defen- ditur.*

Mortuo Jansenio sudarunt mox praela, & opus
quam primum potuit, frustra contranitente Nun-

…te them. Hence arose complaints and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of criticizing episcopal authority, or certainly of showing it too little deference. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on *Hierarchy* under the false name of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work pleased as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed "the most invincible defender of Bishops, the most keen lover of truth, the most just vindicator of Hierarchy, and a Theologian educated in the bosom of ancient theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength for him to prefer to remain hidden for long in such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush invaded his face, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate for ancient theology in a book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the

———— page break ————

Faith, in which, to pass over other errors, he says of the Trinity: "God was not alone before the creation of the world: for He lived in a holy Society of three divine persons, the Father, etc." What then? Is God distinct from the Persons? Further, to him, "the Church is a Society of those who serve God in the light and profession of the true faith, in the union of charity." But sinners do not have charity: are they, therefore, not of the Church?

But to pass over other fragments, the Treatise of Augustine on Virginity, which he had edited with notes in the French idiom under the name of P. Seguenot, a Priest of the Oratory, was fatal to him. For on account of this, and also because he could no longer contain himself, he was arrested by order of Cardinal Richelieu, together with Seguenot, in the same year and month in which Jansenius had passed away, May 14, and was consigned to prison. Released from it after the death of the Cardinal, without doing anything further, he was struck by apoplexy shortly after and departed to the majority on October 11, 1643.

Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed "the most invincible defender of Bishops, a most keen lover of truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, a Theologian educated in the bosom of ancestral Theology." The modesty of Sancyranus did not have enough strength to prefer to remain hidden for longer amidst such praise of himself and his work. But once the Author was discovered, a blush invaded his face, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book: *Gallia Christiana*.

He truly proved himself a Candidate of ancestral Theology in a book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Theologia Familiaris, seu brevis explicatio mysteriorum Fidei*

———— page break ————

in which, to be silent about other errors, he says concerning the Trinity: "God was not alone before the creation of the world: for He lived in a holy Society of the three divine persons, the Father, etc." What then? Is God distinct from the Persons? Next, for him, "The Church is a Society of those who serve God in the light and profession of the true faith, in the union of charity." But sinners do not have charity: are they therefore not part of the Church?

But to pass over other shreds, the Treatise of Augustine on Virginity, which he had edited with notes in the French idiom under the name of P. Seguenot, a Priest of the Oratory, was fatal to him; for on account of this, and also because he could no longer contain himself, he was arrested by order of Cardinal Richelieu together with Seguenot, and cast into prison on the 14th of May in the same year and month that Jansenius had died. After the death of the Cardinal, he was dismissed from prison, but without initiating anything further, he was struck shortly after by an apoplexy and went to the majority on October 11, 1643.

Noailles was further terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In 1727, several bishops had gathered at Embrun to defeat the monstrous errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances they had incited. Furthermore, there were two primary acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer, from the monastery of Saint Genevieve, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who set out for England to carry out the system of Dupin and distinguished himself there with other writings regarding the ordinations of Anglican bishops; and second, the sentence passed on September 20th against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as Quesnel’s work was commended, the Bull condemning it was prostituted as worthy of all execration. demned by the bishops; he himself was summoned to the council to give an account. Soanen initially prevaricated, naming thirteen bishops before whom he would plead his case, and against whom he himself had nothing to object; finally, he set out for Embrun, not without an irreverent retinue, and not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. Then, when asked by the Council whether that was his Instruction, he indeed denied that it had been drafted by him; nevertheless, he openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved of it as his own, until he could be convinced of the errors the bishops had condemned in it. In truth, the stubbornness of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was forbidden from all functions, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. Osiander is mistaken, and indeed childishly, who thinks that the flesh of Christ itself is one thing in spiritual eating or is eaten one way, and another in sacramental. But if it is the same flesh of Christ, therefore it is received by the same mouth, with the same teeth, by the same stomach; namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. And that reason, or the mouth suitable for eating the flesh of Christ itself, is faith. What then? Osiander is mistaken, and indeed childishly so, in thinking that the flesh of Christ itself is one thing in spiritual eating, or is eaten as one thing, and another in sacramental eating. But if the flesh of Christ is the same, therefore it is received by the same mouth, with the same teeth, into the same stomach: namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by the mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. Harduin de Péréfixe, elevated to the Archbishopric of Paris in the same year, was among the first to publish the mandate of subscription throughout his diocese, and in the following year, 1665, he inspects Port-Royal both in Paris and in the countryside, and casts out the Virgins who were resisting more ferociously, together with Agnes of St. Paul, the sister of Arnauld and Abbess of the convent, and shuts them in various monasteries, and interdicts the others from the Sacraments.

It is easy to divine with what sense of pain the faction saw its nest disturbed so suddenly. First, there was huge trepidation, then cries: on one side the torments and mournful laments of those deploring the persecution of truth and innocence; on the other side, curses of those condemning whatever there was of sacred and profane dignity: finally, there was tumult among the very parts of the faction, and it was contested for many years of the present century. For since they were being urged everywhere to subscription by the constant vigilance of the Bishops

and by the severe command of the King, the rigid Morality of many suffered no small stain; they subscribed, without laying aside the error in their mind, they perjured themselves, so that they might be allowed to retain their own for themselves, or aspire to new things. Those who were, or wished to seem, of a more tender conscience, looked around for subterfuges and means by which they might mitigate the horror of perjury, and took refuge in equivocations and mental restrictions, which even the most lax Morality might shudder at. Obtemperatum sine mora, itumque Lugdunum Batavorum Aprili mense; brevi autem mutato consilio in agrum Leodiensem digressi prope castrum quoddam confederunt, ubi mox se minus tutos rati, urbem ipsam ingressi sunt, feque ibidem ad finem usque Augusti paucissimis consciis continuerunt; quando jactationem exosi contemto periculo Bruxellas iterum post semestre spatium furtim reversi, antiquas latebras petierunt, e quibus teste Quesnello ipso in suis quibusdam literis toto quadriennio, quo Arnaldus supervixerat, pedem non extulerunt. I, to speak of myself, promise that under no circumstances—as I have plenty—will I allow you to labor under any lack of familiar things. I judge that all those who loved you for your own sake know this about you. Farewell.

Being reduced to poverty (which I see happens to many), I have been bearing my fortune with a somewhat broken spirit. But since all my studies, which were done by doing good to many, have fallen into ruin, I cannot be sufficiently satisfied. I could never bring my mind to be treated badly by those for whom I was always frugal and liberal. You know well enough what benefits and services our citizens have received from me. How grateful they have been to me, time itself has taught. For when men, whom I had made my friends for my own well-being, conspired against me, and had suborned judges and instructed false witnesses against me, who defended my rights? Or who wished to protect my dignity? But I deservedly feel that this happens, so that I experience those to be ungrateful, in whom

there was no thought for me in loving them. For I know and understand that it is true, which is in the old proverb, that all who fall into a trap for the sake of others, absolve themselves at their own risk. And if the matter were to return to its original state, I would certainly regret having done this. Meanwhile, I am suffering the penalty. But this is nothing to them. I wrote this to you, not so that in a desperate matter I expect your counsel and support, but because I seem to relieve my pain when I speak with you about my inconveniences. Farewell.

You do not write to me of a new matter, nor one unknown to me. Confess to his name because it is holy: they tell of his wonders in the age. Glory to the Father.

### ¶ Monday
### ¶ Nocturn

**O** Lady, let the splendor of your face be my illumination: and may the serenity of your grace shine upon my mind. Exalt my head over my enemies and I shall sing: I will chant a psalm to your name. Do not turn your face away from me: because I have desired your hope and beauty from my youth. I have loved you, O Queen of Heaven, and I have sought your mercy: and do not withdraw your grace from your servant. I will confess you among the nations: and I will honor the throne of your glory. Glory.

**I** will cry to you, O Lady, and you will hear me: you will gladden me in the voice of your praise. Have mercy on me in the day of my distress: and in the light of your truth deliver me. Blessed be you, O Lady: in all the ends of the globe of the earth. The sanctuary which your hands have strengthened: is the holy temple of your body. Your pure and immaculate conscience is the place

———— page break ————

of propitiation and the holy dwelling place of God. Offer to our Lady, O children of God: offer praise and reverence to our Lady. Give strength to your servants, O holy Mother: and blessing to those praising and glorifying you. Hear the groanings of those sighing to you: and do not spurn the vows of those invoking your name. May your hand be prepared to succor me: and your ear attentive to my supplication. May the heavens and the earth, the sea and the circuit of the lands bless you.

I will exalt you, O Lady, because you have taken me up: you will deliver me from the unjust adversary. Turn to me and bring me to life: lead me back from the gates of death: and from the waves of tribulations that have surrounded me. For your own sake and the magnificence of your right hand, crush and dissipate all my adversaries. And I shall offer you a sacrifice of praise: and I will more devotedly exalt your glory. Exult, O heavens, and rejoice, O earth: because Mary consoles her own through her brothers: and will have mercy on her poor.

In you, O Lady, I have hoped, I shall not be confounded forever: in your grace, take me up.

### ¶ Monday
### ¶ Nocturn

**M**ay your face, O Lady, be my illumination: and may the serenity of your grace shine upon my mind. Exalt my head over my enemies and I shall sing: I will chant a psalm to your name. Do not turn your face from me: for I have longed for your hope and your beauty from my youth. I have loved you and sought your mercy, O Queen of Heaven: and do not withdraw your grace from your servant. I will confess you among the nations: and I will honor the throne of your glory. Glory.

**I** will cry out to you, O Lady, and you will hear me: you will make me joyful in the voice of your praise. Have mercy on me in the day of my anguish: and deliver me in the light of your truth. Blessed be you, O Lady: in all the ends of the orb of the earth. The sanctuary which your hands have strengthened: is the holy temple of your body. Your conscience is clean and immaculate, the place

———— page break ————

of propitiation and the holy dwelling-place of God. Offer to our Lady, O sons of God: offer to our Lady praise and reverence. Grant virtue to your servants, O holy Mother: and blessing to those who praise and glorify you. Hear the groaning of those sighing to you: and do not despise the vows of those invoking your name. May your hand be prepared to succor me: and may your ear be attentive to my supplication. May heaven and earth bless you: the sea and all the orbs of the earth.

I will exalt you, O Lady, for you have taken me up: you will deliver me from the iniquitous adversary. Turn to me and vivify me: lead me back from the gates of death: and from the waves of tribulations that have surrounded me. Because of your own self and the magnificence of your right hand: crush and dissipate all my adversaries. And I will offer to you a sacrifice of praise: and I will more devoutly exalt your glory. Exult, O heavens, and rejoice, O earth: for the Virgin consoles her own: and she will have mercy on her poor.

In you, O Lady, have I hoped, let me not be confounded forever: in your grace, take me up.

 I write to you concerning greater things than those I wrote to you about before, for they are such that they not only invite you to read them, but they also possess great weight. The greatest preparations are being made, such as perhaps have never been heard of in our city. Great fleets of ships are being hired, most instructed squadrons are being readied, they are building new triremes, they are preparing for a huge war on sea and land, against a people that has always been most hostile to us. And the hope of all is that there has never been a time given to us in which victory could be better obtained, and if we have obtained it, there will be eternal peace for our city. For all peoples (this one excepted) who could wage war on us have been defeated by us, both by love and by arms, and their strength is nothing other than what remains of our republic, so that we may also curb this nation, which will not be difficult for us to do, provided that speed is applied to our counsels. We have all things that can easily provide victory to our efforts. The enemy is surprised, we are protected by counsel. He

———— page break ————

is impatient, we are most instructed in all necessary things. He is already broken and weakened by domestic and foreign wars, we are whole and never more powerful than now. What more? Many cities have defected from the faith and alliance of our enemies. The strength of our allies increases daily before the cities. There is nothing, therefore, why we should not hold this victory in our hands. We want nothing to be lacking to us. But I also hope well for the timing itself, since we have never used more prudent or stronger men for completing such a matter. I have written this to you; see that you do not divulge anything of these things that would interest the state. But I did not want you to be ignorant of this, so that, as I knew you to be someone who cared most, you might become more learned through me about the greatest things which are being agitated here. First, Osiander cooks up the argument of the Apollinarian heretics and directs it against us in this place, who attribute the Godhead to the flesh of Christ as the soul to the body. Secondly, Osiander’s own similitude overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as the Soul does not exercise all its operations through the body even when hypostatically united to it, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like, so neither does the Godhead of Christ complete all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is everywhere present.

They complain that we tear apart one person of Christ, as Nestorius used to do. First, Osiander rehashes the argument of the Apollinarian heretics and directs it against us in this place, [he] who attributes Deity to the flesh of Christ just as a soul [is attributed] to a body. Next, the very likeness of Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ.
